papers.title: α-synuclein seed amplification assay positivity is associated with motor progression in the prodromal stage independent of phenoconversion
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: -Synuclein seed amplification assay (Syn-SAA) has emerged as a promising biomarker for detecting underlying -synuclein pathology and predicting phenoconversion in prodromal Parkinson's disease (PD). However, its association with longitudinal clinical progression during the prodromal stage remains unclear. We investigated whether baseline Syn-SAA status and kinetic parameters were associated with motor and cognitive progression and subsequent phenoconversion in prodromal individuals. Methods: Clinical progression was assessed using the Movement Disorder Society-Sponsored Revision of the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III motor scores, Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) stage, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores. Linear mixed-effects models were utilized to examine the associations between baseline Syn-SAA status, kinetic parameters, and longitudinal changes in these clinical measures. Additionally, time-to-event analyses were performed to assess the associations between SAA measurements and phenoconversion to PD or dementia with Lewy bodies. Results: We identified 2,532 participants with available baseline Syn-SAA status in the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) prodromal cohort. This longitudinal study, which included up to 12 years of follow-up, comprised 1,714 Syn-SAA-positive and 818 Syn-SAA-negative individuals. Over the follow-up period, Syn-SAA-positive participants exhibited significantly faster motor progression measured by MDS-UPDRS Part III motor score than Syn-SAA-negative participants (0.611 vs. 0.139 points/year; P<0.001). This association persisted after excluding phenoconverters (0.430 vs. 0.202 points/year; P=0.014) and restricting follow-up to seven years (0.588 vs. 0.137 points/year; P<0.001). Among the 1,796 participants included in the time-to-event analyses, 181 phenoconversion events occurred. Baseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with a significantly higher hazard of phenoconversion (adjusted hazard ratio 5.72, 95% confidence interval 3.78-8.68; P<0.001), whereas kinetic parameters showed no significant associations with phenoconversion risk. Conclusions: Baseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with accelerated motor progression during the prodromal stage independent of phenoconversion. These findings support the potential utility of Syn-SAA positivity as a prognostic biomarker for motor progression and phenoconversion, with implications for risk stratification and participant selection in future disease-modifying trials.

papers.title: Modifiable and Context-Specific Factors Associated with Dementia in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: A Community-Derived Cross-Sectional Study
papers.abstract: Background: Evidence linking social, behavioral, and environmental factors to dementia in Central Africa remains limited. Objective: To examine associations between 16 factors and dementia status in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and quantify incremental model fit beyond age and sex. Methods: This cross sectional analysis included 721 participants (232 cognitively unimpaired; 489 with dementia, including 247 with suspected Alzheimers disease). Logistic regression jointly modeled 16 factors, age, sex, and missing-category indicators. Continuous covariates with missing values were mean-imputed and standardized. Model fit was assessed using Nagelkerke pseudo R squared, likelihood-ratio testing, and 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Results: Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 increased from 0.106 with age and sex to 0.368 after adding the factors (change in R2 = 0.262; bootstrap 95% CI: 0.241-0.371; chi-square(27) = 163.62, p < 0.001). Poverty (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.34, 95% CI: 1.52-3.60), low resilience (aOR = 1.84, 95% CI: 1.18-2.86), and depression (aOR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.02-2.31) were associated with higher dementia odds. Higher education (aOR = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.39-0.66, per standard deviation increase) and obesity (aOR = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.10-0.90) showed inverse associations; obesity data were 79.9% missing. Alcohol consumption and PM2.5 exposure were not significantly associated with dementia. Conclusions: Poverty, lower resilience, depression, and education were associated with dementia status in this nonrepresentative cohort. Incremental model fit does not quantify preventable dementia burden, and causality cannot be inferred from these cross-sectional data.

papers.title: Evaluating the Clinical Utility of a Brief Remote Speech Assessment for Screening and Triage of Speech Disorders
papers.abstract: Purpose: Speech abnormalities can often be early or clinically important manifestations of neurologic disease, yet access to clinicians with specialized expertise required for comprehensive motor speech evaluation may limit timely assessment. Brief remote speech assessment could provide a scalable approach for identifying patients who warrant more comprehensive evaluation, but its utility across heterogeneous speech presentations remains unclear. This study evaluated the validity and clinical utility of the Mayo Speech Test (MST), a brief (~5-minute) audio-recorded remote speech assessment, relative to a comprehensive in-person motor speech examination (~1-hour). Specifically, we examined whether MST could support clinically meaningful screening and triage decisions by distinguishing normal from abnormal speech and identifying the presence of a speech disorder. Method: One hundred participants completed a comprehensive in-person speech evaluation and a remote MST. Participants were excluded when the interval between assessments exceeded 90 days (n = 13) or either rater judged audio quality insufficient for diagnostic interpretation (n = 6), with overlapping exclusions resulting in a final analytic sample of 82 participants. Remote recordings were independently evaluated by two speech-language pathologists (SLPs) who were blinded to participant identity. In-person evaluation classifications served as the clinical reference standard and were grouped as normal (n = 33), dysphonia only (n = 5), or speech disorder (n = 43). One participant could not be classified. Performance was evaluated for two clinically motivated binary decisions: distinguishing normal from abnormal (such as dysphonia or speech disorder; Tier 0) and identifying normal speech or dysphonia only versus speech disorder (Tier 1). Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, agreement, and error patterns were examined. Results: Both remote raters demonstrated similar overall performance despite differing error profiles. For Tier 0 screening, Rater 1 demonstrated 93.6% sensitivity and 71.9% specificity for identifying abnormal voice/speech, whereas Rater 2 demonstrated 78.7% sensitivity and 93.9% specificity. For Tier 1 identification of speech disorder, sensitivity and specificity were 83.3% and 86.5%, respectively, for Rater 1 and 71.4% and 97.4% for Rater 2. Interrater agreement was 79.7% for Tier 0 ({kappa} = 0.60) and 86.1% for Tier 1 ({kappa} = 0.72). Missed speech disorders represented an important source of error, with differences between raters indicating distinct thresholds for assigning abnormality and speech-disorder classifications. Conclusions: A brief remote speech assessment showed promising performance for broad clinical classification, particularly when used to address screening and triage questions rather than reproduce the diagnostic granularity of a comprehensive examination. Similar overall performance across raters masked meaningful sensitivity-specificity tradeoffs, highlighting the importance of examining error profiles in addition to aggregate accuracy. MST may therefore have clinical utility for identifying patients who warrant comprehensive motor speech evaluation, but should not be considered a substitute for a full diagnostic assessment.

papers.title: Adverse Events and Baseline Psychological Distress Among Dementia Family Care Partners in the Tele-STELLA Study
papers.abstract: Background: Adverse event (AE) narratives may reveal physical and psychological challenges experienced by family care partners of people living with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Objective: To characterize care partner AEs during the national Tele-STELLA study and explore differences in baseline psychological characteristics by AE category and subcategory. Methods: This descriptive, exploratory analysis included 43 AEs reported by 36 care partners. Narratives were classified as Physical, Psychological, or Random/Other. Baseline depressive symptoms, grief, and behavioral reactivity were compared between care partners with and without each AE type within this sample. Results: Physcial events accounted for 48.8% of AEs, Psychological events for 39.5%, and Random/Other events for 11.6%. Infections predominated among Physical events; stress/distress accounted for half of the Psychological events. Psychological AEs were associated with higher baseline grief and behavioral reactivity. Stress/distress-related AEs were associated with higher depressive symptoms and reactivity, whereas aggression-related Aes were associated with greater grief. Conclusions: Care partner AE narratives captured heterogeneous physical and psychological experiences. Classification may complement conventional assessments of care partner health and distress. These exploratory findings do not establish causality or predictive validity and warrant prospective study.

papers.title: Central motor cortical repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation at 5 Hz or 10 Hz combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation for ataxia in multiple system atrophy of the cerebellar type: a retrospective cohort study of efficacy and predictors of response
papers.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the efficacy of central motor cortical repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) at different frequencies (5 Hz and 10 Hz) combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation on the core domains of ataxia in patients with multiple system atrophy of the cerebellar type (MSA-C), and to explore the independent predictors of the response. Methods: In this retrospective study, 48 patients with a confirmed diagnosis of MSA-C were included. All patients received bilateral cerebellar hemispheric 1 Hz rTMS as background therapy and were divided according to the frequency of central cortical stimulation into a control group (cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation only, n=15), a 5 Hz combination group (n=16) and a 10 Hz combination group (n=17). Ataxia severity before and after treatment was assessed with the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS); absolute improvements and improvement rates were calculated for each subscore and for the total score. Continuous variables were described as mean +/- standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range) according to normality; within-group pre-post comparisons used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and between-group comparisons used one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis H test with Bonferroni correction. Clinical response was defined by an absolute improvement threshold (delta-ICARS total score >= 8 points), and independent influencing factors were analysed by Firth-penalised logistic regression; sensitivity analyses were performed with a total-score improvement rate >= 20% (and with >= 15% and >= 30% as alternative thresholds), and robustness results are reported for the delta-ICARS >= 10-point criterion. Missing cognitive and mood scale scores were imputed by multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; m=5; the mean of the five imputations constituted the analysis dataset) and then included in the analysis. Subgroup and interaction analyses were performed according to the median disease duration (2 years) and median age (57 years). Results: After treatment, the ICARS total score in the overall cohort was significantly lower than at baseline (median difference 7.0 points, P = 20% was used to define clinically significant efficacy, the response rates of the three groups were 6.7%, 50.0% and 58.8% (P=0.006), and both the 10 Hz and 5 Hz groups were significantly better than the control group (Bonferroni-corrected P=0.006 and P=0.040), with no statistically significant difference between the two frequencies. Domain-specific comparison showed statistically significant between-group differences in both the absolute improvement and the improvement rate of limb kinetic function (P=0.013 and P=0.005), with the 10 Hz group significantly better than the control group. When clinical response was defined as delta-ICARS >= 8 points, the response rates of the three groups were 20.0%, 56.2% and 64.7% (P=0.029); Firth-penalised multivariable regression showed that baseline ICARS total score was an independent predictor of clinical response (OR=1.076, 95% CI 1.013-1.143, P=0.017), whereas 5 Hz (OR=4.298, 95% CI 0.757-24.412, P=0.100) and 10 Hz (OR=5.847, 95% CI 0.885-38.640, P=0.067) stimulation did not reach independent statistical significance after adjustment. When response was defined as delta-ICARS >= 10 points, the response rates were 0%, 43.8% and 47.1% (P=0.007), and there were no responders in the control group. Subgroup analysis showed a significant group-by-age interaction (P=0.020); the clinical response rate of patients aged >= 57 years receiving 10 Hz stimulation was 85.7% (exploratory finding; small subgroup sample). The group-by-duration interaction was not statistically significant (P=0.210). Conclusions: Central 5 Hz and 10 Hz rTMS combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation both significantly improved the symptoms of ataxia in patients with MSA-C, and the efficacy was domain-specific, with the greatest improvement in the limb kinetic domain; sensitivity analyses across multiple criteria (delta-ICARS >= 8 points, improvement rate >= 20%, delta-ICARS >= 10 points) consistently supported the efficacy benefit of high-frequency stimulation in the same direction, but stimulation frequency did not reach independent predictive statistical significance after adjustment, and baseline ICARS total score was significantly associated with absolute improvement. Age may have a modifying effect on the efficacy of stimulation frequency (exploratory finding; small sample). This study provides preliminary support for the efficacy of the central 10 Hz combined with cerebellar 1 Hz regimen; the optimal stimulation parameters and independent predictors remain to be verified in larger prospective studies.

papers.title: Traumatic microbleeds are associated with unfavorable outcome out to 1 year after mild traumatic brain injury
papers.abstract: Importance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are commonly observed in mild TBI (mTBI). However, questions remain regarding their long-term prognostic significance. Objective: Determine whether traumatic microbleeds predict unfavorable outcome after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) Design: The prospective longitudinal observational Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury (TRACK-TBI) study enrolled acute TBI patients presenting to Emergency Departments (ED) at 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers between 2/26/2014-08/08/2018. CT and MRI were evaluated using the National Institutes of Health National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH NINDS) TBI Common Data Elements. Outcome was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended (GOSE-TBI) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury. Setting: 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers Participants: 929 GCS 13-15 patients at least 17 years of age (38.5 +/- 16.5 years, 66% male) who underwent clinical head CT =5) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months Results: Generalized estimating equation models showed that TMBs and/or IVH were strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI =5) at 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury, but not with incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI =5 TMBs surpassed the importance of all demographic and baseline clinical predictors throughout the 1-year follow-up period. For prediction of incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8), brain contusions, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and subdural hematoma were more important throughout the 12-month follow-up period. Conclusions and Relevance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are common in mTBI. The presence of 4 or more TMBs and/or IVH is strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5) after mTBI out to at least 1 year, even after controlling for other neuroimaging abnormalities and demographic and clinical predictors. Better understanding of the implications of TMBs for long-term functional outcome may inform rehabilitation planning.

papers.title: Changes in Resting-State Functional Network Specialization in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
papers.abstract: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by heterogeneous clinical presentations and disruption of distributed neural networks. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) provides a systems-level approach to examine intrinsic brain connectivity and may offer insights into disease-related network dysfunction. In this study, we compared rs-fMRI connectivity measures between individuals with PSP and healthy controls and explored differences across PSP clinical variants. 23 participants with probable or possible PSP and 23 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent structural and functional MRI. Graph theory metrics and functional connectivity measures across seven canonical resting-state networks were analyzed. Clinical severity was assessed using the PSP Rating Scale (PSPRS) and cognitive measures including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and frontal assessment battery (FAB). Compared with controls, participants with PSP demonstrated significantly reduced global network modularity and segregation, indicating decreased functional network specialization. Functional connectivity was significantly reduced in multiple large-scale networks, including frontoparietal control, default mode, dorsal attention, somatomotor, and visual networks. No significant differences in graph theory metrics or network connectivity were observed between PSP clinical variants. These findings suggest that PSP is associated with widespread disruption of intrinsic functional networks, reflected by reduced modular organization and network segregation across several canonical resting-state systems while preserving local nodal clustering and global efficiency. Network-level alterations appear broadly similar across clinical variants, supporting the concept that PSP represents a distributed network disorder.

papers.title: Normative Modeling of Structural and Diffusion MRI for Epilepsy Diagnosis and Classification
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Normative modeling expresses an individual's brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus. Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested. We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy. Methods: We retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania. Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references). White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts. Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis. Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (=0.05). Results: We included 273 patients with epilepsy (203 focal, 37 generalized, 33 unclassified; 97 drug-resistant, 176 drug-responsive) and 32 with functional seizures. In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level normative measure distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy; AUCs did not exceed 0.62, with upper confidence limits up to 0.72. In the secondary analysis, whole-brain morphometric deviation burden was modestly higher in epilepsy than in functional seizures (AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.74) but did not separate the within-epilepsy comparisons. The study could detect AUC [≥]0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, [≥]0.64 for focal versus generalized, and [≥]0.60 for drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy. Discussion: Univariate normative deviation summaries from clinical MRI do not currently distinguish these groups well enough to guide care. Whole-brain deviation burden, the only summary measure that differed after correction, was detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification. Progress may require network-targeted analysis of patient-specific deviations and multimodal integration.

papers.title: Plasma Proteomic Identifies GDF15 as a Candidate Lithium Treatment Response Biomarker in Mild Cognitive Impairment: A Secondary Analysis of the LATTICE Randomized Clinical Trial
papers.abstract: Lithium (Li) demonstrates neuroprotective effects relevant to Alzheimer disease (AD). However, its molecular mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized. This study analyzed plasma proteomic profiles from the Li as a Treatment to Prevent Impairment of Cognition in Elders (LATTICE) randomized clinical trial to identify markers associated with amyloid beta pathology, disease progression, and response to Li treatment. In the LATTICE trial, 80 older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) were randomly assigned to receive either low-dose Li carbonate or placebo for two years. Longitudinal plasma samples were analyzed using the NULISAseq CNS Disease Panel 120 proteomic panel. Baseline protein levels were compared according to randomized treatment assignment, amyloid beta PET status, and MCI subtype. Analyses included longitudinal changes in protein levels associated with treatment and time, associations between baseline protein levels and subsequent cognitive, functional, and neuroimaging trajectories, and the influence of baseline protein levels on Li treatment effects. Among the 80 participants, 62 had amnestic MCI and 21 were positive on amyloid beta PET. Baseline proteomic differences were more strongly associated with amyloid beta PET status than with randomized treatment assignment. Plasma p-tau217 concentrations were elevated in individuals who were positive on amyloid beta PET and remained significant after false discovery rate correction. Over time, CALB2 and TREM2 exhibited nominal treatment-by-time interactions in the full cohort, while in the amnestic MCI subgroup, CALB2, TREM2, and amyloid beta 40 demonstrated nominal effects. None persisted after multiple-testing correction. GDF15 showed the most consistent associations with CDR Sum of Boxes trajectories and treatment-effect modification that remained significant after false discovery rate correction in the amnestic MCI subgroup, whereas p-tau217 was most consistently associated with hippocampal volume trajectories. Other protein-outcome associations were exploratory. Plasma proteomics identified distinct molecular patterns associated with amyloid beta pathology and the MCI phenotype, along with exploratory evidence of Li-associated protein changes. Plasma GDF15 and p-tau217 emerged as potential markers of clinical progression and treatment-response heterogeneity, warranting validation in larger, adequately powered trials.

papers.title: White Matter Pathway-Specific Effects of Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation on Vergence Motor Strategy and Binocular Stability
papers.abstract: Objective: Clear vision across viewing distances requires the eyes to achieve binocular alignment and hold it steady. Alignment can be established through smooth dysconjugate eye movement, vergence, alone or in conjunction with rapid saccades. The circuits governing movement strategy and subsequent gaze holding remain less understood. Methods: We used subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) to probe these components in 23 participants with Parkinson disease (PD), comparing binocular eye movements with stimulation on and off and relating behavioral changes to modeled stimulation anatomy. Results: Combined saccade vergence responses predominated in both stimulation states, but individual strategy changes were associated with stimulation location. Greater field of Forel coverage was associated with reduced saccade assisted divergence, and stimulation anatomy helped predict individual changes in this movement strategy. Greater right associative STN coverage correlated with shorter convergence latency. The clearest group effect emerged after movement ended; DBS reduced gaze-holding variance by 37.0% after convergence and 29.4% after divergence, an overall reduction of 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 13.7 to 49.3%; p=0.008). Participants with improved gaze holding had numerically greater modeled exposure to Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways. Conclusions: These findings suggest distinct contributions of associative STN to initiation, consistent with go/no-go control, and Forel pathways to movement strategy. Improved gaze holding raises the novel possibility that stimulation engaging Forel and cerebellar outflow pathways enhances vergence neural integration. Significance: Binocular eye movements reveal how basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways establish movement strategy and sustain alignment, guiding targeted stimulation studies in PD.

papers.title: Circulating Apolipoprotein Profiles and Their Associations with Mild Cognitive and Behavioral Impairment in Older Adults: A Cross-Sectional Study
papers.abstract: Background Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and mild behavioral impairment (MBI) are overlapping prodromal states associated with dementia risk. Circulating apolipoproteins (Apos) may be linked to cognitive and behavioral changes, but their relationships remain unclear. Objective Examine plasma concentrations of multiple Apos in prodromal dementia. Methods This cross-sectional study included 148 Thai participants aged 60-75 years: 56 cognitively normal controls, 47 with MCI without MBI, and 45 with MBI with or without MCI. We measured ApoA1, ApoA2, ApoB, ApoC1, ApoC3, ApoD, ApoE, ApoH, and ApoJ, five lipids, and APOE genotype, and computed an atherogenic Apo composite (ApoB-ApoC1-ApoC3). Primary analyses used multivariable linear regression of quantitative cognitive and behavioral outcomes. Group comparisons were secondary and served to contextualize the dimensional regression findings. Results Across Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) models, 20.7-28.2% of variance was explained by combinations of ApoH, ApoC3, APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status, age, and male sex (inverse associations), and free cholesterol and education (positive associations). The atherogenic composite was inversely associated with MoCA total, memory index, and delayed recall scores, and with Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer's Disease (CERAD) verbal fluency and word list recall. No significant predictors emerged for Neuropsychiatric Inventory (NPI) scores or NPI caregiver distress. All nine Apos differed significantly between groups, with levels highest in MCI, intermediate in MBI, and lowest in controls. Conclusions Circulating Apo profiles differed across controls, MCI, and MBI groups and were more consistently associated with cognitive than behavioral outcomes. ApoH and the atherogenic Apo composite warrant further investigation as candidate biomarkers of early cognitive dysfunction.

papers.title: Cortical surface area is an independent predictor of incident dementia
papers.abstract: Cortical surface area (cSA) is associated with intelligence and cognition, yet structural MRI studies of neurodegeneration in Alzheimers disease and related dementias (ADRD) have emphasized quantification of cortical thickness (cTH) and volume, with very limited evaluation of cSA. We examined whether cSA of AD-relevant brain regions provide diagnostic, prognostic, and biological information beyond cTH and volume across 5,430 participants (3,124 cognitively unimpaired; 1,634 mild cognitive impairment [MCI]; 672 ADRD) from three aging and dementia cohorts: the National Alzheimers Coordinating Center, Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, and Carotids and Minds study. In cross-sectional analyses, cSA and cTH showed weak correlation, and lower cSA was independently associated with greater odds of MCI and ADRD after adjustment for cTH and covariates. Participants with both low cSA and low cTH had greater risk of MCI and ADRD compared to low cSA, cTH, or volume alone. In longitudinal models, baseline cSA predicted incident ADRD independent from cTH, and combined cSA/cTH models outperformed cSA, cTH, or volume alone for predicting incident ADRD over a mean follow-up of 4.3 years. Complementing these findings, proteomics analyses revealed distinct signatures associated with cSA compared to cTH. Overall, these findings support cSA as a clinically informative and biologically distinct dimension of AD-related cortical vulnerability.

papers.title: Greater medial temporal lobe atrophy is associated with less severe cardiac sympathetic denervation in dementia with Lewy bodies
papers.abstract: Background: Cardiac sympathetic denervation varies in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Our previous neuropathological study demonstrated an association between greater Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology and milder cardiac sympathetic denervation in DLB. We investigated whether medial temporal lobe atrophy (MTA), a potential marker of concomitant AD pathology, correlates with cardiac sympathetic denervation assessed by 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) cardiac scintigraphy in probable DLB. Methods: In this retrospective cross-sectional study, we analyzed 162 patients with probable DLB. MTA was assessed by Voxel-based Specific Regional Analysis System for Alzheimer's Disease (VSRAD) Z-scores, and cardiac MIBG uptake by early and delayed heart-to-mediastinum (H/M) ratios. Associations were examined using Spearman and partial Spearman correlations adjusted for age at diagnosis, sex, and disease duration. Sensitivity analyses excluded patients with MIBG-dependent classification, diabetes mellitus or cardiac disease. Results: VSRAD Z-scores correlated positively with early ({rho} = 0.173, P = 0.028) and delayed H/M ratios ({rho} = 0.225, P = 0.004). After adjustment, the association was no longer significant for the early H/M ratio ({rho} = 0.133, P = 0.094), whereas it remained significant for the delayed H/M ratio ({rho} = 0.196, P = 0.013). The adjusted delayed H/M association persisted after excluding 18 patients with MIBG-dependent classification ({rho} = 0.211, P = 0.012) and 40 with diabetes or cardiac disease ({rho} = 0.231, P = 0.011). Conclusions: Greater MTA was associated with relatively preserved cardiac MIBG uptake in probable DLB, particularly on delayed imaging. Consistent with our neuropathological observations, these findings suggest that concomitant AD pathology may contribute to variability in cardiac sympathetic denervation.

papers.title: Inter-articulatory Timing of Vocalic Tongue Body and Jaw Movements across Talkers with Dysarthria due to Various Neurological Conditions
papers.abstract: Purpose: This study compared inter-articulatory timing patterns of the tongue and jaw across talkers with Parkinson's disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Huntington's disease (HD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and neurotypical controls (CON) to identify disease-related differences. The study also explored if a talker's tongue body cycle duration, which serve as a proxy for a talker's habitual speech rate, or a talker's reliance on their jaw, as indicated by their jaw movement amplitude, could predict their inter-articulatory timing patterns. Method: Using three-dimensional electromagnetic articulography, the movements of the posterior tongue and jaw were examined in 24 talkers with PD, 19 talkers with ALS, 18 talkers with HD, 18 talkers with MS, and 34 CON during a sentence repetition task ('Buy Kaia a kite'). The tongue movement during the segment [kai] served as the reference signal (tongue body cycle) for which the phase angle of the jaw reaching the maximum opening position during [kai] was calculated. Tongue body cycle durations were measured as the time between the tongue body movement onset to the tongue body movement offset. The jaw opening amplitude was measured as the relative positional change from the jaw's maximum closing position associated with [k] to the jaw's maximal opening position at the onset of the diphthong [ai]. Results: A significant group effect was found for phase angles. Pairwise comparisons showed that talkers with ALS had significantly larger phase angles than talkers with PD, MS, HD, and CON, indicating a timing pattern where the tongue reached the target [a] earlier relative to the jaw. No significant differences were found for any other pairwise comparisons. Furthermore, no significant associations were found between tongue body cycle durations and phase angles. A significant association was found between jaw amplitudes and phase angles when considering all talkers [rS(110) = .253, p = .008] and when only considering talkers of the control group [r(34) = .361, p = .036]. Conclusions: Findings suggest that during the production of [kai], tongue-jaw timing patterns of talkers with ALS differ from those of talkers with PD, MS, HD, and CON with the tongue reaching the maximum opening position before the jaw while the opposite pattern was observed for talkers of the other groups. However, the variability in tongue body cycle duration did not significantly contribute to the variability in phase angles and the variability in jaw amplitudes only accounted for 6% of the variability in phase angles across all talkers. Future studies are needed to determine if the observed tongue-jaw timing pattern of talkers with ALS generalizes to other phonetic contexts and determine the underlying factors that contribute to the unique tongue-jaw timing patterns of talkers with ALS.

papers.title: Timing of First Poststroke Seizure and Risk of Seizure Recurrence by Stroke Subtype
papers.abstract: Importance: The 7-day cutoff separating acute symptomatic from unprovoked poststroke seizures guides epilepsy diagnosis and long-term antiseizure medication but is consensus based and unvalidated against recurrence risk by stroke subtype. Objective: To determine whether seizure recurrence risk changes abruptly at day 7 and how it varies with first-seizure timing by stroke subtype. Design, Setting, and Participants: This pooled analysis of individual participant data from 36 cohorts in 22 countries (inclusion, 1994-2025) included adults with a first seizure after ischemic stroke, intracerebral hemorrhage, aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, or cerebral venous thrombosis. Exposure: Days from stroke onset (or venous thrombosis diagnosis) to first seizure. Main Outcomes and Measures: The 10-year cumulative incidence of unprovoked seizure recurrence, with death as a competing event, from stabilized inverse probability of treatment-weighted Fine-Gray spline models. Risk zones were based on the likelihood of being helped vs harmed and the 60% epilepsy threshold of the International League Against Epilepsy. Results: Of 2434 individuals (median [IQR] age, 63 [49-75] years; 1181 [48.5%] female), 684 (28.1%) had a seizure recurrence. Risk changed gradually with first-seizure timing, without a day-7 transition; overall 10-year risk differed by subtype (cerebral venous thrombosis, 44%; intracerebral hemorrhage, 43%; ischemic stroke, 40%; subarachnoid hemorrhage, 35%; P < .001). At day 7, the 10-year risk was 24% (95% CI, 17%-32%) after ischemic stroke, 30% (95% CI, 22%-38%) after intracerebral hemorrhage, 41% (95% CI, 22%-53%) after subarachnoid hemorrhage, and 58% (95% CI, 44%-71%) after cerebral venous thrombosis. The 60% threshold was crossed from day 71 after ischemic stroke, day 41 after intracerebral hemorrhage, and day 9 after cerebral venous thrombosis; after subarachnoid hemorrhage, only seizures on days 2 to 3 exceeded it. Mortality was inversely related to recurrence risk. Of 800 first seizures after day 7 following ischemic stroke or intracerebral hemorrhage, which would qualify as epilepsy under current criteria, 335 (42%) had a recurrence risk below the 60% diagnostic threshold. Conclusions and Relevance: In this pooled analysis, seizure recurrence risk after stroke rose gradually, not abruptly at day 7, and differed by subtype. After external validation, subtype-specific risk zones could inform individualized decisions about long-term antiseizure medication.

papers.title: Loneliness is associated with 15-year risk of stroke: The Framingham Heart Study
papers.abstract: Psychosocial factors are promising candidates as modifiable risk factors for stroke. Loneliness is of interest given its rising prevalence worldwide; yet the temporal relationship of loneliness with subsequent stroke remains unclear. Aim: To clarify the association between timing of loneliness and incident stroke. Methods: Framingham Heart Study participants free of stroke with at least two assessments of loneliness prior to incident stroke (at baseline exam, and at prior exam up to 15 years before baseline) were included. Loneliness was assessed using response to the I felt lonely item on the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale, defined as feeling lonely for 3 days within the past week. The recency of loneliness was defined as prior loneliness (present at the prior exam) and baseline loneliness (present at the baseline exam). The primary analysis tested separately for associations between prior loneliness vs no prior loneliness, baseline versus no baseline loneliness, and incident stroke, with 15 years of follow up. Cox models were adjusted for age and sex (model 1) and additionally vascular risk factors (model 2), depressive symptoms (model 3), and physical activity (model 4). Interactions between loneliness and age and sex were explored. Results: Among 4307 participants (mean age 62{+/-}10 years, 55% women), 198 (4.5%) had an incident stroke over a median 6.5-year follow-up period. Prior loneliness was reported by 177 (4.1%) and 226 (5.2%) reported baseline loneliness. Compared to participants without prior loneliness, those with prior loneliness had nearly 3-fold increase in stroke risk after adjustment for age, sex, vascular risk factors, depressive symptoms, and physical activity (HR=2.85, 95% [CI] 1.51-5.39). The effect was primarily observed in participants <80 years (mean age 60 years.HR=3.21, 95% CI 1.69-6.13). No increased risk of stroke was observed among participants with loneliness at baseline. Conclusion: Our findings support consideration of loneliness as a potentially modifiable risk factor, particularly in midlife, for incident stroke.

papers.title: In-country cerebrospinal fluid metagenomic next generation sequencing for pathogen detection in Lima, Peru
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe epidemiology of central nervous system (CNS) infections in low- and middle-income countries is poorly characterized due to limited access to specialized neurodiagnostic testing. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) can detect any pathogen in a single hypothesis-free assay but has largely been confined to high-income countries due to cost and infrastructure requirements. We piloted an in-country CSF mNGS protocol in Lima, Peru to assess the feasibility of this approach in a resource-limited setting. MethodsAdults with suspected CNS infection at Hospital Nacional Dos de Mayo were enrolled. CSF mNGS (DNA and RNA) was performed in-country on a benchtop sequencer with half-volume library reactions and cloud-based analysis (CZID). Paired sequencing at a significantly higher depth was performed on a subset of samples in the United States for validation. ResultsAmong 43 participants (median age 48 years; 21% living with HIV), in-country mNGS detected 20 pathogens in 18 samples (42%), of which 65% were not identified by routine clinical testing. Nine of 15 patients treated empirically for tuberculous meningitis were found to have a non-mycobacterial infection. Detected organisms included Toxoplasma gondii, Taenia solium, Treponema pallidum, herpesviruses, and, on deeper sequencing, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus. Deep sequencing recovered four pathogens missed at shallower-depth. ConclusionsIn-country CSF mNGS was feasible in Lima, Peru and recovered a clinically and epidemiologically meaningful spectrum of CNS pathogens, most missed by routine testing. By utilizing available, lower-output sequencers, we overcame a principal barrier to deploying this technology where the burden of undiagnosed CNS infection is greatest.

papers.title: Wearable-based sleep and activity tracking detects Parkinson's disease and associated pathological hallmarks
papers.abstract: Parkinsons disease (PD) is associated with sleep and motor function impairment, even in the early stages. Here, we investigated whether passive wearable-based sleep and activity tracking can detect PD and its associated pathological hallmarks, dopaminergic deficit and -synuclein pathology. Sleep and activity metrics (SAM) were derived from free-living wrist accelerometry data of a U.S. cohort and used to train a machine learning model (SAM-PD) to distinguish persons with PD (n = 133) from healthy controls (n = 26). The model achieved an AUROC of 0.93 and an AUPRC of 0.98, demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability, and generalized without retraining to an independent European cohort (n = 40; 50% PwPD) monitored with a different device (AUROC, 0.95; AUPRC, 0.95). REM sleep duration, walking cadence, and low-level acceleration features were most predictive. Applied to a U.S. at-risk cohort, SAM-PD performed comparably to the resource-intensive Movement Disorder Society (MDS) prodromal PD risk score in detecting dopaminergic deficit (AUROC, 0.86 vs. 0.80; AUPRC, 0.45 vs. 0.46; n = 121; 12.4% prevalence) and -synuclein pathology (AUROC, 0.76 for both; AUPRC 0.50 vs. 0.42; n = 114; 16.7% prevalence). A combination with the MDS score modestly improved detection. Findings support further evaluation of wearable monitoring for PD screening and biomarker enrichment in larger populations.

papers.title: PSEN1 loss-of-function variants do not cause early-onset Alzheimer's disease
papers.abstract: PSEN1 variants are the most common cause of familial early-onset Alzheimers disease (EOAD), but it is debated whether they act through a loss- or gain-of-function. Following a recent report of a duo with EOAD carrying a predicted loss-of-function (LoF) stop-gain variant (p.K109*) in PSEN1, we sought to determine whether PSEN1 LoF variants, as a class, cause EOAD. We identified 45 carriers of PSEN1 LoF variants predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay in the Alzheimers Disease Sequencing Project, UK Biobank, and BioVU databases. None of these carriers had a recorded diagnosis of early-onset dementia, and 17 were older than 65 years at last follow-up with no dementia or AD reported. Re-analysis of the reported AD-associated variant p.K109* revealed a cryptic splice site predicted to produce an in-frame deletion of 5 amino acids (p.K109_L113del). These results suggest that PSEN1 variants must produce an altered PSEN1 protein product to cause EOAD, while true null LoF PSEN1 alleles do not cause EOAD.

papers.title: Monocyte-to-lymphocyte and Platelet-to-lymphocyte ratios in Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundNeuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorders (NMOSD) are a group of neuroinflammatory conditions that affect the nervous system. MLR and PLR are simple inflammatory biomarkers and are studied in many autoimmune and demyelinating diseases. In this study, we investigate the available evidence to determine whether MLR and PLR are higher in NMOSD patients than in healthy subjects. MethodsSystematic review and meta-analysis of studies measuring levels of PLR and/or MLR in both NMOSD patients and healthy controls were conducted. Mean difference (MD) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were used to measure the difference in levels of MLR and PLR between patients and healthy subjects. ResultsFor MLR, the main meta-analysis yielded a pooled MD of 0.125 [-0.114; 0.363]. I2 was 83.8%. Subgroup meta-analysis of age- and sex-matched studies, demonstrated a pooled MD of 0.066 [0.012; 0.12]. For PLR, meta-analysis revealed a pooled MD of 23.99 [6.03; 41.96]. I2 was 82.3%. Subgroup analysis for age- and sex-matched studies for PLR, showed a pooled MD of 14 [-19.68; 47.68]. ConclusionThe main analysis suggests that MLR is not higher in NMOSD patients than in healthy controls. However, subgroup analysis of age- and sex-matched studies and leave-one-out analysis excluding the outlier study showed a statistically significant MLR increase in patients. PLR was found to exhibit a modest increase in NMOSD patients compared with healthy controls. Nonetheless, subgroup analysis of age- and sex-matched studies showed a statistically non-significant increase. Results should be interpreted cautiously. The available evidence is inconsistent and further research is needed.

papers.title: Age and body-mass index account for part of the sex differences in cerebral venous thrombosis
papers.abstract: BackgroundWomen with cerebral venous thrombosis are younger than men and more often present with headache, but these differences have not been adjusted for age or body-mass index, both of which differ by sex. MethodsSingle-center cohort of 219 consecutive adults with confirmed cerebral venous thrombosis admitted in Zurich in 2001-2021. Presentation, imaging and laboratory findings were compared between women and men, and every difference was re-estimated at equal age and body-mass index. Secondary analyses compared functional outcome, residual symptoms and return to work by sex, with an audit of incomplete follow-up. ResultsWomen (132, 60.3%) were younger (47.3 versus 54.9 years) and had a lower body-mass index (25.9 versus 27.8 kg/m{superscript 2}) than men. Headache (72.0% versus 57.5%) and cortical vein thrombosis (14.4% versus 5.7%) were more frequent in women, but neither association persisted after adjustment (odds ratios, 1.17 [95% CI, 0.54-2.54] and 2.05 [95% CI, 0.59-7.06]). Higher platelet counts (+56 x 10/L [95% CI, 26-86]) and elevated acute-phase markers without documented infection (59.1% versus 33.3%; odds ratio, 2.91 [95% CI, 1.44-5.87]) persisted after adjustment for age, body-mass index and calendar period. Among assessed patients (38% at 6 months), functional independence (86.3% versus 87.5%), residual headache, return to work and recanalization did not differ by sex. ConclusionsAt equal age and body-mass index, the female excess of headache and cortical vein involvement was no longer apparent, whereas a higher platelet count and a non-specific acute-phase response remained. Neither translated into a difference in outcome among assessed patients. Clinical Perspective What Is New?O_LIIn 219 consecutive adults with cerebral venous thrombosis, the female excess of headache and cortical vein thrombosis reported by the large registries was attenuated once age and body-mass index were accounted for, whereas higher platelet counts and more frequent elevation of acute-phase markers without infection in women persisted. C_LIO_LIWomen without a sex-specific risk factor resembled men in age and in the frequency of headache, which suggests that part of the female phenotype of cerebral venous thrombosis is a phenotype of young age and reproductive exposures. C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LISex differences in presentation were not accompanied by differences in functional outcome, residual symptoms, return to work, or recanalization among the patients assessed, so sex alone does not identify patients who need a different follow-up. C_LI

papers.title: DxToniaNet: A Neural Network for Estimating the Severity of Leg Dystonia in Children with Cerebral Palsy
papers.abstract: ImportanceLeg dystonia affects 50-80% of children with cerebral palsy (CP), but severity assessment remains subjective and time-consuming. Objective tools are urgently needed to quantify leg dystonia severity in clinical care and clinical trials. ObjectiveTo develop and validate a deep neural network (DxToniaNet) for leg dystonia severity estimation using 2D clinical video recordings. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsWe retrospectively analyzed video recordings of 298 children with cerebral palsy undergoing a seated hand open-close task as part of routine clinical care (Center 1: 193 videos, 720p/30fps; Center 2: 105 videos, 4K/60fps). Videos were rated for leg dystonia severity by a group of 7 experts using the Global Dystonia Rating Scale (GDRS) leg subscore (range 0-40) which has a minimum clinically important difference (MCID) of 4 points. Videos displaying leg dystonia (median expert GDRS score [≥]1) were used to develop and test a machine learning model (DxToniaNet) for estimating leg dystonia severity. Open-source software (OpenPose) estimated bilateral knee, ankle, and toe coordinates, normalized for height and camera positioning, and 69 variance and amplitude features were calculated based on established expert-cited features of leg dystonia. A neural network, DxToniaNet, was developed, trained and validated using 5-fold cross-validation on Center 1 videos before final testing on independent Center 2 videos. Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s){square}Mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and accuracy in differentiating between videos with clinically meaningful differences in GDRS scores were calculated relative to experts median GDRS scores. ResultsWhen estimating experts leg GDRS scores in testing data, the proposed machine learning (ML) model yielded a MAE of 1.71 {+/-} 1.68 and RMSE of 2.21 {+/-} 0.34 (significantly less than the GDRS MCID of 4), and 90-94% accuracy in differentiating between videos with greater than a 4-point difference in the GDRS. Conclusions and RelevanceWe have demonstrated that DxToniaNet can accurately estimate leg dystonia severity compared to experts assessments with a small (clinically insignificant) error margin. Our methodology supports generalizability since DxToniaNet was developed and tested using independent videos datasets from different centers, recorded under different conditions. In the future, DxToniaNet may help facilitate standardized leg dystonia severity estimation in clinical care and clinical trials. Key pointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSCan a deep learning model use clinically-acquired videos to accurately estimate experts leg dystonia severity assessments in children with cerebral palsy? FindingsAn automated deep learning model (DxToniaNet) trained and tested on clinically-acquired smartphone videos of 298 children with cerebral palsy estimates leg dystonia severity with 90-94% accuracy compared to experts assessments. MeaningDxToniaNet is an objective and free tool to estimate leg dystonia severity and may thus help facilitate standardized tracking of longitudinal treatment responses and clinical trial outcomes.

papers.title: Unraveling the Lifespan Trajectory of White Matter Hypointensity on T1-weighted MR Images and Clinical Application in Various Brain Disorders
papers.abstract: White matter hypointensity on T1-weighted MRI (T1-WMHypo), a putative marker of white matter pathophysiological changes, has been less systematically investigated than the widely studied T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (T2-FLAIR) hyperintensity lesions. Here, we built the lifespan normative reference and assessed the clinical significance of T1-WMHypo across various brain disorders using a large multicenter dataset. We first established lifespan normative reference for T1-WMHypo volume by 34,148 healthy individuals (aged 4-85 years). Then, in 7,587 patients across 21 neurological and psychiatric disorders, normative reference-derived deviations revealed disease-specific patterns, with marked deviations in neurological diseases. Deviations of T1-WMHypo volume contributed to differential diagnosis, larger deviations correlated with brain atrophy, cognitive impairment, and poorer outcomes in various brain disorders. Elevated burden of T1-WMHypo volume predicted poor medication response in Parkinsons disease and accelerated disability progression in multiple sclerosis. These associations persisted after adjusting for conventional T2-FLAIR hyperintensity lesions. T1-WMHypo deviations provide an individualized marker of white matter pathophysiological changes, offering novel insights for precision medicine across development, aging and brain disorders.

papers.title: Histological characteristics of the quadriceps muscle and their associations with gait in older adults
papers.abstract: Background/objectiveThere is a paucity of data about muscle morphology in aging adults. We quantified histologic features of the quadriceps muscle and examined their associations with gait function and physical activity in community-dwelling older adults. MethodsParticipants were from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Postmortem sections of the quadriceps muscles were examined by immunohistochemistry using antibodies against myosin heavy chain, and histological characteristics of the quadriceps muscles were derived through images quantifications and segmentations. In addition, brain sections were assessed for collection of Alzheimers disease and related dementias pathologies. Before death, participants physical activity was objectively measured through wearing an accelerometer sensor for 10 days, and gait function was quantified by walking 8 feet and turning 360{degrees} twice. Linear regressions and compositional analyses were used for analyzing data. ResultsPostmortem quadriceps was examined in 236 decedents (mean age at death was 91.7{+/-}6.0 years, and 71.6% (n=169) were females. On average, 44.7% (SD=19.5) of the muscle fibers were type I and 54.2% (SD=19.4) were type II, and 40.6% (SD=13.0) and 21.9% (12.9) of the quadriceps muscle area were composed of type I and II muscle fibers, respectively. In compositional analyses, male sex (estimate=0.303, SE=0.126, p=0.016) and more physical activity (estimate=0.118, SE=0.059, p=0.045) were associated with larger quadriceps muscle areas with type II muscle fibers, which were related to better gait (estimate=-0.049, SE=0.021, p=0.021). Quadriceps muscle composition explained an additional 3.2% of gaits variance beyond the 5.8% variance explained by Alzheimers disease and related dementias brain pathologies. ConclusionQuadriceps muscles having larger areas with type II muscle fibers were associated with more physical activity and better gait function in aging adults. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying these associations are critical for developing new therapies.

papers.title: Robust Feature Engineering Techniques for Designing Efficient Motor Imagery-Based Systems Using Multidomain Electroencephalography
papers.abstract: Motor imagery-based brain-computer interfaces (BCls) have potential applications in neurorehabilitation; however, the high dimensionality and complexity of electroencephalography (EEG) signals present challenges for accurate classification. This study aimed to improve the classification of motor and motor imagery activities using multidomain feature engineering and feature selection on the MILimbEEG dataset. Time-domain, frequency-domain, and wavelet-based features were extracted from 16-channel EEG signals, yielding 416 features. Maximum relevance minimum redundancy (MRMR) was then applied to select the four most informative and minimally redundant features. These features were used to train support vector machine (SVM), K-nearest neighbors (KNN), Na"ive Bayes, and decision tree classifiers, with performance evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation based on testing accuracy, precision, recall, and Fl-score. The Gaussian-kernel SVM achieved the highest testing accuracies of 92.50% for motor activities and 95.48% for motor imagery activities. For the highest-performing motor imagery classification, precision, recall, and Fl-score were 86.97%, 88.33%, and 87.04%, respectively. These findings demonstrate that reducing 416 multidomain EEG features to four discriminative features using MRMR can maintain strong classification performance. The proposed feature-engineering framework may support the development of computationally efficient EEG-based BCI systems for neurorehabilitation applications. HighlightsO_LIMultidomain feature engineering extracts 416 features from 16-channel EEG signals. C_LIO_LIMRMR reduces 416 EEG features to four discriminative features for classification. C_LIO_LIGaussian SVM achieves 95.48% accuracy for motor imagery classification. C_LIO_LIGaussian SVM achieves 92.50% accuracy for motor activity classification. C_LI

papers.title: A Multi-Cohort nnU-Net for White Matter Hyperintensity Segmentation Across 2D and 3D FLAIR Acquisitions
papers.abstract: BackgroundWhite matter hyperintensities (WMH) are increasingly pooled across aging, cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD), and dementia cohorts that differ in both disease composition and FLAIR acquisition. Most automated segmentation tools were developed within a narrower range of populations or protocols, and few have been tested for whether segmentation accuracy and error remain consistent across conventional 2D and isotropic 3D FLAIR, or whether the choice of algorithm alters downstream clinical associations. MethodsWe developed a single nnU-Net model, taking FLAIR and T1-weighted images as inputs, using 460 2D and 3D FLAIR scans from a neurodegenerative cohort (Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, ADNI), a CSVD-enriched cohort with same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR (Washington University White Matter Ischemic-Hypoxia study, WWISH), and a population-based sample (UK Biobank), holding out 92 scans from 66 participants at the participant-level as an internal test set. We further evaluated the model in an independent ADNI3 3D FLAIR set (n = 25), benchmarking voxel-wise overlap (Dice), volumetric agreement, and lesion-level detection against SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and FreeSurfer WMH-SynthSeg, and compared acquisition-specific volume bias in participants with paired 2D and 3D FLAIR. We then compared how WMH volumes from each method predicted incident dementia in cognitively unimpaired adults from ADNI and the Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (n = 1,174; 42 incident cases). ResultsIn the internal test set, the model achieved a mean Dice of 0.73 (SD 0.10), compared with 0.50, 0.57, and 0.29 for SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and WMH-SynthSeg (all FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). Dice was similar on 2D and 3D FLAIR (0.75 vs. 0.71). In WWISH participants imaged with both acquisitions, mean volume bias differed between 2D and 3D scans by 1.8 mL for the model versus 4.7-9.9 mL for the comparators. Advantages were largest in low-burden scans (<5 mL; Dice 0.66 vs. 0.19-0.54) and for lesions of [≤]100 voxels (detection 77-87% vs. 14-63%). In ADNI3, the model retained a mean Dice of 0.70 (SD 0.14) without retraining and exceeded all comparators (FDR-adjusted p [≤] 0.002). Model-derived WMH volume was associated with incident dementia beyond clinical covariates (OR per SD 1.40, 95% CI 1.11-1.77; likelihood-ratio p = 0.009; cross-validated AUC 0.71 vs. 0.68), whereas comparator-derived volumes did not significantly improve model fit. ConclusionsTraining a single model across disease contexts and FLAIR acquisitions yielded WMH segmentation that was similarly accurate on 2D and 3D FLAIR, sensitive to low-burden disease, transferable to an unseen protocol, and clinically informative, supporting its use in multi-cohort, mixed-etiology studies. KEY POINTSO_LIA single nnU-Net trained across neurodegenerative, cerebral small vessel disease, and population-based cohorts and across 2D and 3D FLAIR outperformed SHIVA-WMH, segcsvdWMH, and WMH-SynthSeg, with the largest gains in low-burden scans and small lesions. C_LIO_LIIn same-visit paired 2D and 3D FLAIR scans, the models volume bias relative to acquisition-specific reference masks varied less across acquisitions, whereas comparator biases varied with acquisition. C_LIO_LIOnly WMH volume from the model significantly improved model fit for incident dementia beyond clinical covariates, highlighting the potential influence of segmentation algorithm choice on downstream clinical inference. C_LI

papers.title: Sub-Threshold Stochastic Vibration Improves Fingertip Tactile Sensitivity in Stroke Survivors and Healthy Adults, with Source-Localized EEG Evidence for Cortical Network Reorganization in Healthy Adults
papers.abstract: Cutaneous sensation is vital for daily function and safety, yet it commonly declines with ageing and after neurological injury, with stroke survivors particularly affected. This study investigates whether sub-threshold stochastic (random) vibrations can enhance light-touch (cutaneous) sensation in healthy adults and stroke survivors and characterizes the associated changes in cortical functional connectivity (FC). Nineteen healthy participants and five stroke survivors took part. A custom device delivered sinusoidal and stochastic vibrations to the volar surface of the right middle fingertip. For each participant we first determined the detection threshold for stochastic vibration alone, then the threshold for a 30 Hz sinusoidal vibration, and then the threshold for that sinusoidal vibration combined with imperceptible stochastic noise fixed at 80% of the stochastic threshold; in ten healthy participants a super-threshold combination (120% of the stochastic threshold) was also tested. High-density (64-channel) electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded throughout for the healthy participants. Adding sub-threshold stochastic noise lowered the sinusoidal detection threshold in every participant tested and produced consistent reductions in all five stroke survivors; expressed as gains in sensitivity, individual improvements reached up to 19 times in healthy participants and up to 4 times in stroke survivors. Source-localized EEG showed that sub-threshold stochastic vibration significantly increased FC, most extensively in the alpha band, with prominent involvement of frontal regions (superior and rostral middle frontal cortices and anterior cingulate; cluster-based permutation p < 0.05), consistent with a noise-driven modulation of sensory and attentional networks. Super-threshold noise produced weaker, predominantly beta-band changes, in line with signal masking rather than resonance. These findings indicate that sub-threshold stochastic vibration lowers light-touch detection thresholds and reorganizes cortical connectivity in both healthy and stroke populations, and they support prioritizing cutaneous sensation in stochastic-resonance-based neurorehabilitation for stroke survivors.

papers.title: Longitudinal Cerebrospinal Fluid Biomarker Changes Following Shunt Surgery in Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus - Insights from the Gothenburg POiNT study
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe underlying pathophysiology of idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is incompletely understood and reliable predictors of shunt response are lacking. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers may provide insights into disease mechanisms and help identify patients most likely to benefit from surgery. The aim of this study was to explore CSF biomarker dynamics following shunt surgery and their relationship with clinical outcome. MethodsThe POiNT (Prediction of Outcome in iNPH) was a prospective longitudinal study. One hundred and thirty-five patients with iNPH underwent standardized clinical assessment and lumbar CSF sampling 3.6 (SD 2.1) months before and 5.7 months (SD 2.4) after shunt surgery. CSF was analyzed for biomarkers of astrogliosis, axonal injury, amyloid, and tau pathology, and synaptic dysfunction. Clinical outcomes were assessed using the iNPH scale. Associations between baseline biomarker levels, postoperative biomarker changes, and clinical outcomes were evaluated using adjusted correlation and regression analyses. ResultsIn total, 69% (n=93) improved after shunt surgery. Substantial postoperative increases were observed for most CSF biomarkers: The largest relative increases were seen for growth-associated protein 43 (GAP43) (2.92-fold change), followed by Phosphorylated tau (2.65-fold change), Neurogranin and total-tau (both 2.29-fold change) as well as A{beta}40 (1.93-fold change), and A{beta}42 (1.76-fold change) (all p<0.001). In adjusted analyses, postoperative change in several biomarker levels were associated with degree of clinical improvement. However, baseline biomarker levels generally showed limited predictive value. Lower baseline monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP1) levels were associated with greater odds of overall clinical improvement but had a modest predictive performance (AUC 0.67). No baseline biomarker demonstrated strong discrimination of treatment response. ConclusionShunt surgery was associated with substantial changes in CSF biomarker concentrations, several of which correlated with the degree of clinical improvement. Although baseline levels did not predict clinical outcome, the observed biomarker changes may reflect biological responses to treatment, altered CSF dynamics, or both .iNPH. Future studies examining these processes relating to disease reversibility might help elucidate pathophysiological mechanisms in iNPH.

papers.title: Atrophy-related inflammation CSF markers predict clinical progression in genetic frontotemporal dementia
papers.abstract: Neuroinflammation is increasingly recognised as a key contributor to frontotemporal dementia (FTD) pathophysiology, yet how inflammatory processes relate to neurodegeneration and clinical progression remains poorly defined. This study aimed to identify a multivariate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflammatory signature covarying with brain atrophy, and to determine its relevance to clinical and cognitive outcomes in genetic FTD. We recruited 234 participants (non-carrier controls n=78, presymptomatic carriers n=115, symptomatic carriers n=41) with CSF, MRI, and clinical (CDR (R) + NACC FTLD sum of boxes [CDR-SB]) and executive (Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-Revised Digit Symbol Substitution Task [DSST] assessments. A regularised canonical correlation analysis (rCCA) was used to derive a shared protein-brain covariance axis. Participants were followed annually for up to 8.6 years (CDR-SB) and 11.5 years (DSST), and linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate individual rates of clinical progression (CDR slope) and executive decline (DSST slope). The predictive value of the inflammation- and MRI-based profiles for cross-sectional CDR-SB, CDR slope, DSST and DSST slope were tested in linear models. Due to floor effects and violations of parametric assumptions, Bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals (CI) and bootstrap CIs (95%, 5000 replicates) were utilised as the primary inferential criterion in the 2nd-level linear models; effects were considered non-significant if the 95% BCa CI crossed zero. The rCCA identified a robust inflammation-brain axis (r=0.89, p<0.001), driven by CXCL9, FLT3L, CCL3, and frontotemporal-insular atrophy pattern. In symptomatic carriers, the MRI canonical variate was associated with CDR-SB ({beta}=3.80, CI: [0.64, 6.20]) at baseline, whereas the inflammatory protein canonical variate was predictive of CDR-SB slope ({beta}=0.24, CI: [0.02, 0.46]). Whereas both MRI ({beta}= -7.27, CI:[-14.20, -1.00]) and protein ({beta}= -7.83, CI:[-14.00, -2.16]) canonical variates were linked to DSST cross-sectionally, but not longitudinally. No significant associations were found in pre-symptomatic carriers or non-carrier controls. A data-driven CSF inflammatory signature, covarying with frontotemporal-insular atrophy, tracks with clinical severity and cognitive impairment in people with genetic FTD, highlighting inflammation as a candidate therapeutic target and progression biomarker in the earliest clinically manifest stages of disease.

papers.title: Cross-cohort validation of EEG biomarkers using a pre-registered three-criterion framework: a demonstration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
papers.abstract: BackgroundDespite decades of EEG biomarker development for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), no candidate has progressed to clinical deployment, partly because cross-cohort validation is rare. We aimed to develop and demonstrate a pre-registered three-criterion screening framework to identify which candidate EEG features show the combined properties required for biomarker translation: cross-sectional discrimination, within-subject reliability, and cross-cohort effect consistency. MethodsWe pre-registered a validation framework adapted from FDA-NIH BEST principles and applied it to 18 EEG features across three independent cohorts: EEGET-ALS (six ALS patients, 170 healthy controls; home recordings over 17 days), UCL/Penn State (eight ALS patients; clinic recordings over 1-2 months), and a healthy adult test-retest reference (60 participants, three sessions over one month). Features were required to meet three pre-registered criteria: (1) cross-sectional discrimination (Cohens d > 0.5), (2) within-subject reliability (ICC(3,1) > 0.6 in both ALS cohorts independently), and (3) cross-cohort effect direction consistency. Cross-cohort permutation testing (1000 iterations) and subject-level bootstrap resampling (500 iterations) were applied to assess robustness. ResultsThree features met all three pre-registered criteria: gamma power, theta power, and spectral entropy. Cross-cohort permutation testing showed that no permutation, out of 1000, produced any feature in the three-cohort reliability intersection (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). Bootstrap resampling indicated that the composition of the selected set was sensitive to sample composition (median count 1, 95% CI [0, 4]), with gamma power (67% inclusion), spectral entropy (43%), and theta power (32%) the most stable features at a relaxed reliability threshold (ICC > 0.5); at the primary pre-registered threshold (ICC > 0.6), the corresponding inclusion probabilities are lower (57%, 27%, and 19%, respectively). A principal methodological finding was that cross-cohort differences in feature reliability were large relative to the apparent disease-associated signal, most clearly demonstrated by relative beta power (ICC = 0.09 in a home-recorded cohort versus 0.93 in a clinic-recorded cohort); because recording protocol, hardware, setting, population, and preprocessing all differ jointly between cohorts in this dataset, this is evidence of cohort-associated variability that plausibly includes a protocol contribution, not a separately identified, isolated protocol effect. ConclusionsThis study provides a pre-registered, multi-cohort EEG biomarker screening framework for ALS with explicit bootstrap-quantified uncertainty. Gamma power, spectral entropy, and theta power are identified as priority candidates for prospective validation. A recurring methodological observation is that protocol-related cohort differences appear to contribute more to cross-cohort variability than disease-related effects within this dataset; because protocol is confounded with cohort, equipment, and preprocessing, this pattern is descriptive rather than causal. The observation nonetheless has direct implications for the design of multi-site EEG biomarker studies in neural engineering.
